frameworks.name: Three Types of Business Debt
frameworks.definition: Every business always incurs debt at inception; the three forms are financial debt, management debt (underskilled hires), and technical debt (inadequate infrastructure). The strategic choice is which type to take on first based on ease of repayment.

frameworks.name: Units x LTV Growth Formula
frameworks.definition: Business growth reduces to two levers: sell more units or increase lifetime value per unit. Everything else is complexity layered on top of this identity.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that every business always incurs debt at startup; the only choice is which type to take on. The three forms are financial debt, management debt (hiring underskilled people for the opportunity), and technical debt (lacking infrastructure). Founders should choose the form of debt easiest to repay as fast as possible rather than pursuing a debt-free illusion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Recognizing that all debt forms are unavoidable expands the strategic levers available for structuring a business, because founders no longer rule out debt categories that could be optimal for their situation.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for businesses below $1 million annual revenue, everything comes down to marketing and sales. Product quality matters significantly less at that scale because the business is not generating enough volume for word-of-mouth to propagate meaningfully given the size of the market.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: At sub-$1M scale, the business touches too few customers for product reputation to compound organically via word-of-mouth; marketing and sales are the binding constraint, not product quality.
bounded_by: On the longest time horizon, only product quality matters
Does not apply once word-of-mouth referral volume becomes a meaningful growth driver

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that on the longest time horizon, the only thing that matters in business is product quality: whether the thing delivered in exchange for money is good, and whether customers consistently feel they received the better end of the deal. Marketing and sales without product quality create a perpetual hamster wheel where nothing accumulates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to businesses seeking compounding growth over multi-year horizons
claims.mechanism: Sales and marketing produce new customers but no carryover credit; product quality produces retained customers and word-of-mouth that pay the founder today for work done years ago, compounding without additional acquisition spend.
bounded_by: Sub-$1M businesses can sustain revenue through marketing and sales alone without great product

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that marketing is sales at scale: a business that masters marketing can reach one-to-many with the same persuasion it previously delivered one-to-one in sales calls. However, marketing without product quality is still a perpetual hamster wheel because no accumulated reputation forms.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Marketing multiplies each persuasion unit across audiences, but the compounding loop that makes businesses durable requires customers to stay users or advocates over time, which only product quality generates.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a founder should not add marketing and sales investment to a business until the product is excellent: every customer who buys unreservedly loves the product, referrals arrive every month, and the business grows without paid acquisition. Only then should paid marketing and sales be layered on top.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder seeking to build a large and durable business
Not optimizing solely for short-term revenue
claims.mechanism: Adding marketing before achieving organic referrals masks product problems with paid acquisition, preventing the feedback loop needed to improve the product, and inflates CAC relative to LTV.
bounded_by: Sub-$1M founders focused on cash flow may need marketing and sales before product is perfect

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a million dollars a year in revenue equals approximately $20,000 per week, or roughly $3,000 per day. Business growth reduces to one formula: units sold multiplied by lifetime value per unit. To grow, a business must either sell more units or make each customer worth more.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for founders who are not yet making money, the calendar is the diagnostic tool: any time not contributing to either acquiring new customers or increasing customer lifetime value should be eliminated. If a founder is working every available hour without earning more money, they are working on the wrong activities.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Time is the primary asset of an early-stage founder; every hour spent on non-revenue-generating activity has full opportunity cost with zero return, and eliminating non-contributing tasks creates room for actions that directly drive the two growth levers.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the job of the founder in the early stage of a business is always promotion: letting people know the business exists. Obscurity, not product quality or sales skill, is the primary constraint when a business is starting.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A business that no one knows about cannot generate customers regardless of product quality or closing skill; awareness is the prerequisite constraint that must be resolved before other levers matter.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi describes eight ways to let people know about an offer: four the founder executes personally (warm outreach, cold outreach, posting content, running paid ads) and four that use other people (affiliates, referrals, employees, agencies). These eight channels apply whether a business is doing $1 or $1 billion in revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

anchors.value: 4 channels (warm outreach, cold outreach, content, paid ads)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that warm outreach to existing contacts is the cheapest lead-generation action available to any founder, and the most common contact list is larger than founders realize. Combining phone contacts, sent email history from all accounts, and social media followers across platforms yields at minimum a few thousand contacts for almost any person.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Any founder regardless of revenue stage
claims.mechanism: Each social media follower, email contact, and phone contact has already granted some form of permission for contact; the permission removes the cold-outreach barrier and raises response rate vs. truly cold lists.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that founders with limited resources adopt a high-volume daily outreach target of 100 contacts per day, which requires approximately five hours at 20 outreach attempts per hour. This high-volume approach is justified because time is the primary asset of a resource-constrained early-stage founder.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: At low resource levels, substituting time for money is the only viable lever; 100 outreach attempts per day at any conversion rate generates more absolute leads than lower-volume approaches, and volume also accelerates skill improvement through repetition.
bounded_by: As resources grow, automation and dialers reduce the time requirement per contact

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that asking warm contacts whether they know anyone who might be interested, rather than directly pitching the contact, reduces social pressure and paradoxically increases conversions: roughly nine times out of ten, the contact responds that they themselves are interested rather than referring a third party.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Warm outreach to existing social contacts
claims.mechanism: Asking for a referral removes the pressure of a direct sales pitch, which reduces the contact's defensive posture; because the contact is not being asked to commit personally, they lower their guard and often disclose their own latent interest.

anchors.region: contacts who respond with own interest
contacts who redirect to a third party

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes his personal evolution in business philosophy: early in his career he focused entirely on sales, then discovered marketing as one-to-many sales and became highly skilled at it. He then realized that marketing without great product is a perpetual treadmill where nothing accumulates. Today, Acquisition.com waits until a portfolio business has organically growing referrals and universal customer love before adding any marketing or sales investment on top.

Alex Hormozi illustrates the contact-list exercise for founders who claim they have no one to reach out to: export all contacts from the phone's address book (list one), export all sent-message recipients from every Gmail, Yahoo, and other email account ever used (list two), then export followers from every social platform. He notes that Twitter, Instagram, and TikTok all allow DMs to followers, unlike YouTube. Combining these lists produces what he describes as a very large addressable warm audience even for someone who claims to know no one.

Alex Hormozi shares his own early-stage schedule as an example of disciplined time allocation: when he had fewer resources, he began outreach work around 4 or 5 AM and finished around 10 AM, then started the rest of his day. This ensured that the five hours of highest-leverage promotion activity happened first before any other obligations could displace it.

practices.text: Review your calendar and eliminate every time block not contributing to acquiring more customers or increasing customer lifetime value.
Start daily outreach at 4 or 5 AM when possible so promotion work is complete before other demands compete for the time block.
When asking warm contacts about your new offer, frame the ask as 'Do you know anyone who might be interested?' rather than pitching them directly.
Do not add paid marketing or sales investment to a business until every customer loves the product and organic referrals are arriving monthly.
Choose the type of startup debt (financial, management, or technical) based on which is fastest to repay given the specific opportunity being pursued.
